children: Shares in Shein dropped by as much as 10% during trading in Hong Kong.
Fast-fashion retailer Shein's stock slumped after making its hotly-awaited trading debut in Hong Kong.

Shares in the company, which was founded in Nanjing, China, in 2008 but is now headquartered in Singapore, tumbled by as much as 10%. Shein pared some losses, ending the day with a decline of about 4% at HK$46.58, or $5.94.

Shein started the session with shares priced at HK$48.56, raising HK$13.6 billion and giving it a value by market capitalization of just over $26 billion. Management said in a prospectus filed last week that it was aiming for a market cap of $27 billion.

But this is a far cry from the $100 billion value the discount ecommerce giant once achieved in a private funding round back in 2022 when it first planned its initial public offering in New York and then London.
The fall of over 70% comes as Shein has faced years of concerns over its labor practices, quick product turnover, legal challenges and the worsening of trading relations between the U.S. and China.

The company took a considerable blow in May of last year, when the de minimis exemption - which allowed it to ship cheap goods to the U.S. without paying customs - expired. Also at the start of July this year, the European Union removed its rule that let companies send goods worth less than EUR150 ($174) duty-free.

Shein said in a filing published after its Hong Kong listing that the closure of the loophole in the U.S. had an "adverse impact" on sales in the country and that the change to EU regulations could be "generally in line with or exceed the impact observed in the U.S."
The retailer reported net revenues of nearly $42 billion in 2025, an increase of 8% compared to the previous year.
It also saw net losses of just below $100 million for the first three months of this year.
